World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: $250 tax break for millions in budget's 'rebalance' of system for workers
World.content:
Labor will raise taxes on investment properties and some trust funds, giving the revenue back to workers with a new $250 tax break under reforms it says will "rebalance" the Australian tax system.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has unveiled sweeping changes to negative gearing, capital gains tax (CGT) discount and trusts, and announced a new income tax offset to be paid to more than 13.3 million workers every year from July 2028.

Mr Chalmers described Labor's fifth budget as the "most important and ambitious" in decades, saying it made the tax system "fairer and stronger for workers, businesses, first home buyers and future generations".

Federal budget 2026: Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

"In an era where people feel like the system no longer works for them, this budget doesn't just acknowledge that, it acts on it," he said.

A plan to rein in the ballooning NDIS is the biggest single source of savings in the budget, which is expected to remain in the red over the next four years.

War in the Middle East is forecast to have a significant impact on Australia's economy in the short term, with inflation peaking at 5 per cent in a scenario with oil prices starting to ease from July.

Labor is betting on public support from younger Australians to offset expected political blowback for the decision to break multiple promises made at the 2025 federal election.

It expects the property tax changes will support an additional 75,000 Australians to buy their first home over the next decade.

Jim Chalmers says this year's budget is "ambitious". (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Workers to receive extra income tax break

The budget includes a new $250 Working Australians Tax Offset (WATO) that will be paid annually to taxpaying workers from mid-2028.

The WATO, which Mr Chalmers says is the "biggest cost-of-living measure in this budget" will cost $6.4 billion in the first two years.

Initially, the income offset and separate tax relief for businesses effectively neutralise the extra budget revenue generated by the CGT, negative gearing and trust changes, which are forecast to raise $8.1 billion over four years.

Loading

But over time the government will earn more from those reforms than it spends on tax cuts, with the total tax package improving the budget deficit by an estimated $77.2 billion over a decade.

Mr Chalmers said the government was explicitly "creating space to return bracket creep" to workers with potential further tax cuts in future years.

High oil prices fuel inflation

The global oil crisis sparked by war in the Middle East is forecast to significantly impact the Australian economy in the short term, with growth downgraded by half a per cent to just 1.75 per cent in 2026–27.

Treasury's central forecast has assumed oil stays at about $US100 a barrel until the end of June and then "glides" to $US80 over the following 12 months.

Under this scenario, inflation is expected to peak at 5 per cent in the middle of the year before returning to 2.5 per cent in the following financial years.

But Mr Chalmers warned those figures were "heavily dependent" on events overseas beyond Australia's control, including the length of the Iran conflict and closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

In a more "severe" scenario where the oil price peaks at $200 a barrel and takes three years to fall back down, Mr Chalmers said Treasury has forecast Australia would still "avoid" a recession.

But in this case unemployment would rise to 5 per cent in 2027–28, while inflation would soar to 7.25 per cent.

Budget forecast to remain in red

The budget deficit is now forecast to reach $31.5 billion in 2026–27, which is about $2.8 billion better than was forecast six months ago.

That improvement is despite a $19 billion increase in government spending over the upcoming financial year, with total expenditure now expected to reach $830 billion.

The additional costs include continuing NDIS blowouts, new policy costs in areas like defence and pharmaceuticals, and higher government payments due to inflation.

The spend is offset by a forecast $45 billion improvement to the budget bottom line over the next five years, of which more than 90 per cent comes from revenue upgrades.

Jim Chalmers says housing affordability is a key issue. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Australia's gross debt will climb above $1 trillion this financial year, and grow to $1.25 trillion by the end of the decade.

Unemployment is forecast to tick up from 4.25 per cent this financial year to 4.5 per cent for the next two, assuming the economic shock caused by the global oil crisis peaks at the end of June.

Forecasts over the medium term show total government spending staying at the same level for the first half of the 2030s, eventually declining as NDIS cuts take greater effect.

At the same time, expected revenue increases at a steady rate, surpassing spending in about the mid-2030s.

It's boosted by growing gains from the changes to CGT and taxing trusts, as well as by the usual assumption of no further income tax cuts beyond what is currently in the budget.

The budget has also forecast net overseas migration for the current financial year will be 295,000, dropping to 245,000 in 2026–27 and 225,000 the following year.

Loading

NDIS largest single source of savings

A massive overhaul of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) announced last month is the biggest single source of savings in the budget, worth $37.8 billion over the next four financial years.

A reduction in the private health insurance rebate for older Australians is forecast to save $11 billion over the next decade.

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to this federal budget. Have your say.

Labor has also clawed back unspent funding from what were once flagship initiatives to tackle climate change, pulling a total of $1.3 billion over 10 years from the Hydrogen Headstart, Solar Sunshot and Battery Breakthrough Initiative programs.

The government will also save about $760 million in uncommitted funding from Australia's Economic Accelerator program.

A reduction in public service spending on external labour and other non-wage expenses, like travel, property and hospitality is expected to save $2.7 billion over four years.

The "better targeting" of services for veterans and their families is expected to decrease government payments to providers by $606.6 million over five years to 2029–30.

Tax changes coming for investors and trusts

Australians will no longer be able to negatively gear an investment property purchased after tonight, unless it is a newly built home.

People who currently negatively gear their investment property, which is where any rental losses are deducted from their tax, will be able to continue to do so.

The 50 per cent CGT discount will end, returning to the previous setting of a tax on the profit from the sale of the property or asset, minus inflation.

A minimum tax rate of 30 per cent will be introduced.

Loading

Australians who invest in new homes would retain the option of receiving either the 50 per cent discount or the inflation model, depending on which was lower.

Though the changes will impact all investment properties purchased from budget night onwards, a transition period of one year under the old system will continue until June 30, 2027.

The new CGT and negative gearing settings are expected to generate $1.35 billion in extra revenue for the government in 2028–29 and then $2.28 billion the next financial year.

Treasury expects the tax changes will result in 35,000 fewer dwellings being built over a decade, which would be offset by an estimated 65,000 new builds under a $2 billion local infrastructure fund.

Labor is also introducing a minimum 30 per cent tax on discretionary trusts from July 2028, which is expected to generate $4.47 billion in revenue by the end of the decade.

The tax will not apply to fixed or testamentary trusts, complying superannuation funds, special disability, deceased estates or charitable trusts.

Some types of income, such as from agriculture, will also be exempted.

Labor to defend broken election promise

At the last federal election, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese repeatedly insisted Labor was not looking to touch investment property taxes.

In one exchange, when asked to guarantee there would be no changes to CGT or negative gearing, Mr Albanese said, "Yes, how hard is it? For the 50th time."

Mr Chalmers said such comments reflected the government's "singular focus" on housing supply at that time.

"It … has become increasingly clear to us that even though the challenges in the housing market begin with housing supply, they don't end with them," he said.

"The main change in our thinking is the view that you can't let the intersection of the housing market and the tax system continue to lock out so many people from getting a toehold in the housing market".

Mr Chalmers has acknowledged the tax changes will be "controversial", but insisted they were the right call.

"It would have been easy, but wrong, for a government like ours to see the way that the housing market is developing, see the way the pressures on young people are intensifying and to leave some of these structures unattended to," he said.

Tobacco excise plunges again

Government revenue from tobacco has continued to plummet, with the budget forecasting the tax take from cigarette products will be $1.2 billion less for the 2026–27 financial year than it expected just six months ago.

By 2029–30 it is now expected the tobacco excise will only generate a paltry $2.1 billion, which is about 75 per cent less than the $7.8 billion in tax collected in 2024–25.

Other measures previously announced ahead of the budget include a productivity package that is expected to save $10.2 billion in regulator costs every year.

Labor is also introducing a two-year loss carry back for Australian companies with up to $1 billion in annual turnover, and a loss refundability for startups in their first two years.

The budget includes $53 billion in extra spending on defence over the next decade, including $6.8 billion over the forward estimates.

The government is also changing a tax break for electric vehicles purchased on novated leases to make the popular scheme more sustainable long-term.

Independent economist Chris Richardson said the budget ticked off some "long-overdue changes" on Treasury's reform "to-do list".

"They will have good impacts, especially over the longer term, but they start small and they start slow," he said.

Mr Richardson said the improvements in the budget bottom line in the short term were mostly due to a windfall tax take due to war and inflation.

"It's an old story," he said.

Mr Richardson also warned he was not certain the Reserve Bank of Australia would be able to "ignore" the federal spending, particularly when combined with recent state budgets, in its interest rate deliberations.

"The key for the RBA is the near term, and the coming financial year is set to see rather more government spending than had been estimated a handful of months ago," he said.

World.title: Why Chalmers reined in the property tax lurks in the budget
World.content:
It's unusual for a federal budget to look too far beyond the next election.

Traditionally, the annual gabfest is an opportunity for treasurers to update their promises of distant surpluses — even if they rarely eventuate — before dangling the prospect of a tax cut if you vote for them at the next national poll.

This year is different.

Federal budget 2026: Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has waded into what once was the political no-go zone of winding back tax breaks for the wealthy, backtracking on an explicit promise from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese before the most recent election.

In the past decade, Labor has been trounced twice by voters who overwhelmingly rejected the policies at elections that were theirs for the taking.

The resulting recriminations seemed to have killed any hint of ending the tax lurks around property investment forever.

But now they're back.

One of the more striking elements from the now well-entrenched program of pre-budget leaks is the lack of outrage from the population or even the opposition.

Broken promises aside, the blowback from critics has been decidedly muted, mostly restricted to complex arguments about the potential for a shortage of rental properties.

Rage against the machine

Across the developed world, the political establishment is under siege.

In the US and across Europe, voters for years have been gravitating from the centre to the extremes.

Now it's happening here as the nation witnessed last weekend in the Farrer by-election, a result that underscored the extent of erosion in Coalition support, in the very seat where the Liberal Party was born.

Negative gearing, CGT and trusts explained The government is poised to make changes to negative gearing, the capital gains tax discount and the tax treatment of trusts. So how do they work, and what could changes look like?

Labor, despite its thumping majority, is under the same pressures as voters look for alternatives.

The drivers may be different in each country, but the underlying forces are the same.

As former US Democrat advisor James Carville once quipped: "It's the economy, stupid."

In the US, globalisation wreaked havoc on the workforce, as entire industries pulled stumps and shifted offshore.

In Australia, the growing sense of alienation and dissatisfaction among younger generations of workers who have found themselves priced out of the property market has become palpable.

Ignoring the obvious undercurrent among the fastest-growing cohort within the electorate is a great strategy for any party in pursuit of extinction.

The pendulum swings

When it comes to budget coverage, debt and deficits usually dominate the headlines.

But budgets, and fiscal policy in general, are far more than a mere book-balancing exercise.

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to this federal budget. Have your say.

They also incorporate powerful tools that redistribute wealth and income within society, usually via the tax system.

Australia has long been a country with a "progressive" tax system where those on higher incomes pay a higher proportion of their pay in taxes.

As a result, they usually pay a great deal more.

For most of the past quarter century, however, the pendulum has swung back towards workers rather than those who earn a buck from investment.

Loading

On top of lucrative superannuation incentives, which delivered higher income groups much bigger tax discounts on contributions and tax-free income upon retirement, property investment became a beacon for those looking to build wealth.

But it was negative gearing, which allows investors to deduct losses from rental properties from their salaries, combined with a heavily discounted capital gains tax bill on profits from the sale of investment properties that has most enraged the youth.

Real estate has quadrupled in value over the past 25 years, well above the growth in wages.

The lurks have also cost the nation dearly.

According to a 2024 Treasury study, negative gearing was expected to cost the budget $7.7 billion this financial year in foregone revenue. Added to the expected $5.87 billion in lost revenue on the capital gains tax discount, that's a total of $13.57 billion.

The benefits of those foregone cash receipts overwhelmingly accrue to the nation's highest income earners.

The end result? Australia is home to some of the highest-priced real estate on the planet.

Loading

Will the budget changes work?

Handing out tax incentives is easy. Clawing them back is not.

The changes already have been erroneously described as tax hikes rather than the curtailing of tax benefits.

According to the budget statements, the changes to both negative gearing and capital gains tax will pull in just $1.35 billion in the first year and $2.3 billion in the second.

Loading

That's a long way short of the cash Treasury reckons is lost on the tax incentives, mostly explained by the decision to grandfather the changes.

Those with existing investment properties will continue to reap the gains of negative gearing, while the original capital gains tax arrangements will also remain in place until a hybrid system kicks into place after the changes are introduced next year.

Without the grandfathering, the political backlash would have been more severe, given the 1.2 million negatively geared property households.

It also would have had the potential to send property prices into a sharp decline.

While most first home buyers would welcome a sharp drop, it could have caused some issues with a real estate-obsessed banking system.

The mooted changes are likely to have only a modest impact in the early years and gradually increase as older investors sell.

World.title: How CGT changes could push investors to look outside property
World.content:
Investors in the share market are undercompensated for the impact of inflation under current capital gains tax (CGT) settings, according to the budget.

As expected, the federal government will scrap the flat 50 per cent CGT discount for investments for more than 12 months, a measure largely sold as addressing intergenerational housing inequality.

But the budget also highlighted the potential to shift investment away from existing properties and into stocks and new properties.

"The reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax are expected to improve the efficiency of investment decisions, as they are more likely to be made for economic reasons rather than tax outcomes," the budget read.

Federal budget 2026: Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

Stock investors had raised concerns about CGT changes ahead of the budget, including younger Australians who had invested in shares instead of property due to being locked out of the housing market.

Established private investor Liam Walsh holds $3 million of high-growth shares, chasing capital gains.

"I'm looking for some tissues to cry into because nearly all of my income that I derive comes from capital growth," he told The Business.

Liam Walsh supports CGT changes despite expecting to take a financial hit. (ABC News: Adam Wyatt)

Despite expecting to take a personal hit on the reform, Mr Walsh supports the policy.

" I think it's a really good policy. It sucks for me because I'm going to lose money. "

Broadly, however, data in the budget showed that investors in the Australian share market have been undercompensated for the impact of inflation by the current CGT settings.

The CGT discount does not appropriately compensate investors in the share market, according to the budget. (Supplied: Treasury, ASX, ABS)

For example, inflation made up 56 per cent of asset price growth for ASX 200 shares held for 10 years to March 2026.

For the broader All Ordinaries index, inflation accounted for 53 per cent of growth.

Over the same period, inflation accounted for 38 per cent of asset price growth for all property, meaning the flat 50 per cent discount would overcompensate for inflation.

Loading...

Devika Shivadekar, an economist at consultancy firm RSM Australia, said the CGT changes would likely incentivise people to think about other methods of wealth building outside of property.

"Australians' obsession with building property portfolios has, over time, created an inequity between the haves and the hopefuls," Ms Shivadekar said.

"In isolation, CGT changes might cost share investors, but it will likely encourage people to look for investments outside of property."

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the current system was encouraging investors to "pile into existing housing, pushing prices up, and blocking people out of the housing market, particularly younger people".

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the opposition would not be supporting the changes to negative gearing or the CGT discount.

'From tax advantages towards market-driven returns'

Jacki Neumann, the head of capital markets at investment app Sharesies, described the changes as signalling "a structural transition in how Australians are incentivised to build wealth".

"By moving the needle from tax advantages towards market-driven returns, the focus for the everyday investor shifts from navigating tax structures to evaluating the fundamental quality of their investments," Ms Neumann said ahead of the budget.

The government is aiming to move investors towards new property and shares. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

However, the changes will "change the equation" for growth investors, she added.

"While a move toward an indexation framework aims for a more equitable environment, it creates a threshold where the tax benefits of indexation diminish once an asset's growth significantly outpaces inflation.

" This shift invites a recalibration of risk, where investors will need to weigh their appetite for high-growth assets against the more predictable returns of income-generating investments. "

UBS equity strategist Richard Schellbach agreed that the CGT changes, combined with the winding back of negative gearing, could see stocks "improve their relative appeal" compared to property investments.

In a note to clients ahead of the budget, he said that would increase the relative appeal of income stocks, which pay a reliable dividend, over growth stocks.

Government to consult with startup sector

In the lead-up to budget night, some high-profile investors had argued that scrapping the 50 per cent CGT discount could hurt startups, which often use employee share schemes.

Startups utilise share schemes to attract talent, offering a potentially lucrative payday should the company succeed, making up for their inability to match the bigger salaries of more established competitors.

Employees would then be liable to pay tax on any capital gains made if they sold their shares.

The budget acknowledged "the unique characteristics of the tech and startup sector" and flagged a period of consultation ahead.

" The government will consult on the interaction of the capital gains tax reforms and incentives for investment in early-stage and startup businesses. "

Loading

Tax changes to help business cash flow

The government has also introduced measures to lessen the tax burden on smaller businesses, as they face inflationary pressures from the Iran war fallout.

The ability of businesses with turnovers up to $10 million to instantly write off assets up to $20,000 will be made permanent, giving firms certainty rather than waiting for yearly extensions.

For example, a restaurant investing $18,000 in a new deep fryer and $2,000 on new furniture can immediately reduce its taxable profit by $20,000, rather than having to claim those assets over several years.

Small businesses can continue to claim refunds for tax losses against previously profitable years. (Supplied: rawpixel.com)

The government estimated it will save small businesses around $32 million in compliance costs each year.

"We're making tax time simple for small businesses, which will save them 376,000 hours a year," Mr Chalmers said.

The budget also contained reforms aimed at improving cash flow for small-to-medium businesses.

"It helps with cash flow when you need it most. A business having a rough year doesn't just need sympathy, it needs actual cash," Ms Shivadekar said.

Mr Chalmers said that change is aimed at "bolstering resilience and risk-taking".

Around 85,000 companies will now be able to "carry back" losses from the current tax year to obtain a refund of taxes paid on profits in the previous two years.

The government said the permanent scheme would benefit mostly small businesses, with companies turning over up to $1 billion a year eligible for refunds.

"It's particularly valuable for businesses in cyclical industries that may have had profitable years recently but are now feeling the squeeze," Ms Shivadekar said.

"It's the norm in most developed countries."

It will cost $890 million to deliver over the next five years.

Josh Ball, the co-founder of produce subscription service Farmers Pick, welcomed the loss carry back being made permanent.

"With business there's a whole set of risks that we play into, and being able to have that somewhat de-risked or be able to have that flexibility, really enables businesses to sustain challenging periods such as shocks with fuel and fertiliser," he told The Business.

The government will consult the startup sector on the impact of CGT reforms. (Unsplash: Annie Spratt)

So that startups, which are unlikely to have turned a profit yet, do not miss out, an additional budget measure will allow businesses to claim refunds for tax losses in their first two years of operation.

Coming in from July 2028, the so-called loss refundability measure will be capped at the amount a startup has paid in fringe benefits tax and withholding tax paid on employee wages.

The government said the business tax reforms in the budget were "expected to support investment, innovation, risk-taking and resilience".

World.title: Australia's last baby boomer prime minister becomes King of the Kids
World.content:
In all likelihood, Anthony Norman Albanese will be this country's last baby boomer prime minister.

But he has now officially donned the cape of Youth Warrior, addressing himself to the unwinding of policies that for decades have plumped his own generation's asset sheets with tidy two-bedders, sure-fire flippers and solid family homes (close all facs, public transport).

This moment has been coming for some time, as home ownership rates ebbed among the young and swelled among the old, and as the massed ranks of millennials and gen Zs eligible to vote gradually approached and then outnumbered baby boomers.

Federal budget 2026: Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

The prime minister was born into exceedingly modest circumstances, but like many in his cohort, he caught a few breaks over his lifetime.

He received a free university education and caught the Sydney real estate wave at the right time. Of the 226 present serving members of the parliament, he's one of a handful who've been around long enough to be on the "old" parliamentary super scheme, guaranteeing a handsome income for life.

And tonight he becomes the first serving prime minister in decades to take a hammer to the most sacred shibboleth in Australian domestic politics: the assumption that housing in Australia is not just a life essential fairly high on Maslow's hierarchy of needs, but also an investment opportunity that presents, to the shrewd operator, a lower-taxed path to wealth than the orthodox technique of having a job.

In all likelihood, Anthony Norman Albanese will be this country's last baby boomer prime minister. (Facebook: University of Sydney)

An 'ambitious' budget

The buzzword across the 2026 budget and the introductory speech delivered by the treasurer is "ambitious". And it is indeed an ambitious thing for a government to shut down tax breaks that have earned a great many people a great deal of wealth.

What's steeled the prime minister, apart from his impatient treasurer, is the growing sentiment among younger generations (who are also the voters with the most elections in their future) that they are getting the rubber end of the real estate plunger. That they are priced out of the real estate market, obliged to pay ludicrously high rents to landlords who, thanks to a heady admixture of advantageous tax settings and timing, are sometimes holding multiple properties.

The language of generational change is everywhere in this budget. Private health insurance concessions for the over 65s are to be whipper-snipped to the tune of $3 billion. A wholesale redraw of annual migration now explicitly prioritises "educated, higher-skilled and younger migrants", particularly those who are already studying or living in Australia.

Venture capital incentives are henceforth to favour "young, expanding firms". Twenty thousand small companies will be able to trouser refunds of fringe benefits and payroll tax, so long as they've been in operation for less than two years.

Tax breaks for electric vehicles, meanwhile, will be eased back gradually, because in the assessment of the budget's drafters, the electric vehicle industry is now "mature", and if there's a coda to this document, it's that if you're mature, you're probably ticking along OK.

'Prospective' property and investment tax breaks

The property and investment tax breaks aren't being turned off like a tap, of course. The changes are "prospective". New capital gains tax rules don't kick in until July next year. New tax arrangements for discretionary trusts come into effect a year after that — in July 2028 (by which time, presumably, if everything goes according to plan, Albanese will be riding toward election victory aboard a palanquin toted by young and muscular voters, while Angus Taylor or his replacement reedily vows to restore justice to tax minimisers, to an appreciative rattling of Zimmer frames).

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to this federal budget. Have your say.

Properties currently being negatively geared can still be negatively geared. This is thanks to the practice of "grandfathering" — a budgetary practice in which persons currently benefiting from a scheme are allowed to continue benefiting, in order to avoid mass panic and/or systems collapse.

"Grandfathering" is a term absolutely crying out for a rebranding, by the way. And not just because in the context of this "intergenerational justice" budget, it sounds a lot like making an exception for Grandpa and his 15 blocks of flats.

"Grandfathering" as a term dates back to the United States in the late 19th century, when various Southern states introduced new barriers to voter enrolment (literacy requirements, property requirements and so on). Voters whose grandfathers had been eligible to vote before the Civil War — and if you stop for a moment to consider what colour skin such citizens would universally have, the gambit becomes clear — were exempted from the new rules. So yeah, "grandfathering" does have rather an unfortunate historical connotation of the joke continuing, to some degree, to be on the disadvantaged.

Millennial and generation Z voters now constitute a majority of the electorate. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Will Australians cop giving up sweet tax breaks for fairness?

But the biggest post-budget challenge facing Albanese: King of the Kids™ isn't going to be about the etymology of "grandfathering".

Albanese now faces the knottiest advocacy task of all: Convincing voters to accept a short- and mid-term hardship (the forfeiture of sweet tax breaks) in the interests of long-term fairness and prosperity.

The task is made more difficult by the fact that the Australian population is already deeply cheesed off. And by the fact that he literally just promised one year ago that he would absolutely not do the thing he's just done. AND by the fact that even the youthful beneficiaries of this ambitious redesign are not sitting quietly around radiograms, ears pricked for the good news of how the old guy in the Billy Bragg T-shirt has just taken up the cudgels on their behalf. Which is why we must all prepare for the days ahead, which will be full of Tim Wilson TikToks depicting Albanese as a Boomer who's filled his beak with tax breaks and publicly funded super, and now is pulling up the drawbridge behind him, breaking not only his solemn promise but also the hopes and dreams of teenage investors everywhere.

Loading

This is a test of advocacy, of persuasion and — indeed — of ambition. Also, of political identity.

For the Liberal Party, the encouragement of home ownership is a bone-deep value.

When Robert Menzies gathered the disparate anti-Labor forces together at Albury 82 years ago, preparatory to forming the Liberal Party, his evocation of Australia's "Forgotten People" was already laced rhetorically around the family home, which he deemed "the foundation of sanity and sobriety … the indispensable condition of continuity; its health determines the health of society as a whole".

Over his prime ministership, Menzies initiated cash handouts to first home buyers. Built houses. Encouraged the sale of public housing stock to tenants. Home ownership rates soared from 53 per cent to 77 per cent.

But just days ago, Albury voted for One Nation. So, either the Liberal Party isn't saying the right things on this issue, or it's saying them in the wrong language, or to the wrong people.

Which is why this particular moment, in Australia's history as a federation, is so extraordinarily a) challenging and b) interesting.

World.title: Your five-minute guide to this year's cost-of-living budget measures
World.content:
Here we go again. Another federal budget has been handed down.

In Canberra, Treasurer Jim Chalmers described helping Australians with the cost-of-living crisis as one of the government's key priorities.

"We understand this crisis [Middle East] is adding to the cost-of-living pressures facing Australians," he said.

"That's why we are taking some of the sting out of global price rises."

Federal budget 2026: Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

So what exactly is in the budget to help Australians feeling the pinch from the global oil shock?

Here's a super-quick guide to the cost-of-living relief.

Permanent $250 tax offset for workers

The government is delivering another tax cut for Australian workers by introducing the Working Australians Tax Offset (WATO).

The WATO will provide an annual tax offset of up to $250 for income earned by Australian workers from the 2027–28 income year.

This increases the effective tax-free threshold by nearly $1,800 to $19,985 for workers, or up to $24,985 for workers eligible for the Low Income Tax Offset.

It will benefit more than 13 million Australian workers.

The WATO will help Australian workers keep more of what they earn.

Loading...

Combined with the first three tax cuts already legislated, an Australian worker on average earnings ($81,245) will receive a tax cut of $1,978 in 2026–27 and $2,496 per year from 2027–28, compared to 2023–24 tax settings.

$1,000 instant tax reduction

From 2026–27, a new instant tax deduction of up to $1,000 will simplify work-related expense deductions.

The reforms will allow workers to knock $1,000 off their taxable income without providing receipts.

This will help workers cut back on the paperwork and save them time and money at tax time.

The deduction will deliver 6.2 million workers (42 per cent of taxpayers) an average tax saving of $205.

Jim Chalmers says the cost-of-living crisis is exacerbated by the Middle East war. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Taxpayers claiming more than $1,000 in work‑related deductions will still be able to do so in the usual way.

Charitable donations and other non‑work-related deductions will continue to be claimed on top of the instant tax deduction, as will union or other trade, business or professional association memberships.

Extra tax cuts

Additional tax cuts will arrive in 2026 and 2027, adding to the first round of tax cuts, which began in July 2024.

From July 1, 2026, the 16 per cent tax rate, which applies to taxable income between $18,201 and $45,000, will be reduced to 15 per cent.

From July 1, 2027, that rate will drop again to 14 per cent.

How much will the average-earning Australian save with all the government's tax benefits? The combined benefit to an Australian worker on average earnings of the government's three tax cuts, new tax offset and instant tax deduction will be up to $2,816 from 2027–28. Averaged out over the year, the three tax cuts, instant deduction and the new offset are the equivalent of up to $54 back in the average earner's pocket each week.

That means if you're earning the average income of $79,000, you will see an additional tax cut of $268 in 2026–27 and $536 per year compared to 2027–28.

The total tax cut from 2027–28 onward would be $2,190 per year.

"These tax cuts will provide cost-of-living relief and return bracket creep, building on tax cuts that took effect in 2024," budget documents said.

An Australian worker on average earnings is expected to pay up to $38,977 less tax from 2024–25 to 2036–37, relative to 2023–24 settings.

Increasing Medicare levy low-income threshold

The government will increase the Medicare levy low-income thresholds for singles, families, seniors and pensioners by 2.9 per cent from the 2025–26 income year.

This will benefit more than 1 million Australians on lower incomes who will continue to be exempt from the Medicare levy or pay a reduced levy rate.

The WATO will provide an annual tax offset of up to $250 for income earned by Australian workers. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Cheaper medicines

The federal government is investing $5.9 billion to deliver cheaper life-saving medicines to Australians through new listings on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS).

This includes treatments for cystic fibrosis, chronic kidney disease, various cancers and more.

The maximum general co-payment under the PBS will also be reduced to $25 and the concessional rate will be frozen at $7.70 until 2030.

The budget will also permanently subsidise COVID-19 oral antiviral medicines through the PBS.

Other cost-of-living measures

Potential home buyers Read more It's a stressful time for anyone hoping to break into the property market, with Australia's longstanding housing shortage making homes unaffordable for many. But there is some relief for prospective homeowners, especially young people and families. The government is reforming negative gearing and capital gains tax (CGT) concessions, which is expected to help 75,000 Australians into the housing market over the next decade. For more information, ABC senior political correspondent Jake Evans has more here. Fuel excise Read more In news that won't be new to Australians, the government has delivered a $2.9 billion package to more than halve the fuel excise and reduce the heavy vehicle road user charge to zero for a three-month period. In total, the rate of excise on petrol and diesel has been reduced by 32 cents, cutting the cost of a 65-litre tank of fuel by nearly $23. Paid parental leave Read more On July 1, 2026, the Australian government's Paid Parental Leave Scheme will be expanded to six months. The budget documents say families will be $14,000 better off than they would have been in 2022. More bulk billing Read more The government has invested $11.4 billion to incentivise bulk-billing. The goal is to ensure nine out of 10 GP services are bulk-billed by 2030. Health care for women Read more In this year's budget, Keytruda has been listed on the PBS to treat cervical cancer. Without the subsidy, patients could pay more than $15,400 per script. The government is also investing $2.7 million to list new items on the Medicare Benefits Schedule for participating midwives to provide long-acting reversible contraceptive services. Public dental services for adults Read more For the first time the government will permanently fund the Public Dental Services for Adults agreement. This is to support the delivery of dental services to eligible adult patients to the tune of $431 million. The public dental fund is generally for low-income adults and eligibility is determined by each state and territory.

What's in the budget for pensioners?

In this year's budget, Mr Chalmers didn't call out any measures that were specifically for people on the age pension.

However, there are two key items that could have an impact:

Cheaper medicines

Medicare levy thresholds

For eligible older Australians, the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine Arexyv will be listed on the National Immunisation Program at no cost to patients.

The government will also invest $3.7 billion to deliver more beds, more packages and better care for older Australians to ensure they get the support they need. This includes 5,000 additional aged care beds each year, specifically for those with limited financial means.

In a pre-budget speech at the National Press Club, Health Minister Mark Butler announced more than 3 million Australians aged over 65 would have to pay hundreds of dollars more for their private health insurance a year.

The government argues this will re-establish fairness between generations.

World.title: Negative gearing cut off for existing homes bought after tonight
World.content:
Tax perks that have been used by property investors for decades to maximise profits and offset their losses will be restricted from tonight, in one of the most significant changes to the tax system in years.

Restrictions to negative gearing from this evening and capital gains tax (CGT) discounts from July 2027, and the closure of a family trust loophole, will shift how Australians are taxed in the favour of workers.

And the government expects it will move 75,000 properties from the hands of investors to homeowners, slow house price growth and eventually lead to lower rents.

Federal budget 2026: Look back at how the day's events unfolded with our blog.

The tax changes will lead to about 35,000 fewer homes being built, Treasury expects, though other taxpayer-funded measures will boost supply and lead to an overall increase in housing stock of about 30,000.

Negative gearing Read more From the evening of May 12 (budget night), new property purchases will not be eligible to use negative gearing unless it is a newly built home. Previously if the costs of a rental property (such as mortgage interest, repairs and rates bills) exceeded the rental income it generated, those losses could be deducted from a person's income tax and reduce how much tax they paid. Loading Now that benefit will only be claimable for existing investment properties purchased or exchanged before May 12, and will come into effect from July next year. Investors will still be able to deduct losses from rental income, and carryover rules will allow excess losses in one year to be deducted from a future year where a profit is made from rent. Capital gains tax discount Read more From July 2027, a discount that halves the tax owed on any profit made from selling shares, investment properties or other assets held for more than a year will end. From that date, assets will instead owe tax on any profits made beyond inflation. Or, put another way, only the amount of inflation over the time an asset was held from 2027 will be deducted from the tax a person owes. Loading And to ensure people cannot carefully time the sales of their assets to minimise the tax they owe, a 30 per cent minimum tax rate will apply to any capital gains made. Any assets held before July 1, 2027, will still have the old rules applied — meaning the 50 per cent tax discount will be applied. If those assets are sold after July 2027, the next tax scheme will be applied to any capital gains accrued after that date. People can choose for that amount to be calculated based on either a valuation of the asset as at July 1, 2027, or using a formula that apportions tax owed by the time held under each tax scheme.

But it constitutes a breach of faith with voters, who were promised at last year's federal election that a re-elected Albanese government would not do anything that could hurt supply, including tampering with negative gearing or capital gains tax.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the tax changes would shift who benefited from new housing supply.

"The tax system got out of whack, and we are trying to align it," Mr Chalmers said.

"It has become increasingly clear to us that even though the challenges begin with housing supply, they don't end there.

"We can't let the intersection of the housing market and the tax system continue to lock out people from getting a toehold in the housing market, particularly young people."

Jim Chalmers says it is worth breaking a promise to voters for the right reasons. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Chalmers said it was worth breaking a promise to voters if it was done for the "right and justifiable reasons".

" It would have been easy but wrong to see the way the housing market is developing, to see the way the pressures on young people are intensifying and to leave some of these structures unattended to. "

Alongside the changes to housing tax perks, a minimum tax rate of 30 per cent will also be applied to family trusts, ensuring people using them are not doing so to pay a lower rate of tax than they otherwise would.

Loading...

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the tax changes would lead to 35,000 fewer homes and higher rents, all while the budget forecasts increases to net migration.

"At the end of the day, the government has put forward a budget that is about broken promises, higher taxes, lower livings standards and fewer homes," Mr Wilson said.

"By the government's own admission it will lead to fewer homes being built … we won't be supporting these measures."

Negative gearing ends for established dwellings bought after tonight

Currently if a landlord's expenses, including mortgage interest, repairs and rates bills for a home, exceed the income from tenants, those losses can be deducted from their taxable income.

Under the new scheme, established properties purchased after tonight will no longer be able to use negative gearing to reduce income tax.

Investors who already own properties will be exempt, along with purchases of new builds.

New builds are dwellings constructed on vacant land or where an existing property was demolished and replaced with a greater number of dwellings.

Knock-down rebuilds or substantial renovations that do not increase supply will not be eligible.

The government says the housing market needs rebalancing, with investors now making up about double the spending on housing compared to first home buyers.

Loading

Treasury estimates 83 per cent of that investor credit is going towards existing housing, not helping bring on new supply.

"Where people are negatively gearing in the future, we want that to be for new homes," Mr Chalmers said.

After tonight, anyone buying an existing dwelling will still be able to deduct rental losses from the income generated by their residential property investments, with a carry-forward measure allowing excess losses in previous years to be deducted from rental income in future years.

The new rules will apply to all established dwellings exchanged after tonight, and will commence from July 2027.

CGT discount overhauled, but guaranteed 30 per cent minimum tax

Under the current scheme, any profits made when an asset is sold are counted towards a person's taxable income, though only half of that profit is counted if the asset has been held for more than a year.

Under the new scheme, tax is owed on any profit made from an asset's sale beyond growth from inflation.

So if a property's value grew in a year by 5 per cent, and inflation in that year was 3 per cent, tax would be owed on the 2 per cent growth in value above inflation.

And no matter what income tax a person owes, their tax payable on that profit can never be less than 30 per cent, closing a loophole that could allow someone to pay no tax on profits from selling properties, shares or other capital gains.

Pensioners and others receiving income support will be exempt from that minimum 30 per cent rate.

And as is currently the case, a person's main residence is exempt from capital gains tax.

Loading

The new rules will apply to all assets purchased after July 1, 2027. For any assets purchased before that date and sold after it, any gains made before July 2027 will be taxed under the old system and any gains made after July 2027 will be taxed under the new system.

Taxpayers will be able to choose whether to seek a valuation of the asset at July 1, 2027, or calculate tax owed based on the time the asset was held under each scheme (meaning if an asset was held equally under both, half the profit would be calculated under the old scheme and half the profit under the new scheme).

The CGT discount restrictions also end a long-running exemption on assets before 1985, which will also become subject to tax on any gains made after July 2027.

Individuals investing in new builds will be able to continue to choose between claiming the 50 per cent discount or the inflation rate.

And the government says it will consult with the tech sector on how CGT should be applied to startups to ensure the new tax settings do not suppress innovation.

35,000 drop in supply from tax change to be offset by public spending

The negative gearing cut-off is expected to lead to a net 75,000 homes being sold by investors to owner-occupiers over 10 years, which the government says is equivalent to reversing a decade's worth of decline in home ownership rates.

However, the fall in investor demand will also have a small impact on housing supply, reducing new supply by about 35,000.

Treasury expects that drop in demand to also cause a temporary slowing in house price growth, which for the capital cities was already at 0.3 per cent last month.

The negative gearing and capital gains tax changes are expected to slow house price growth by about 2 per cent a year in the near term, and cause a $2 per week increase to median rents, or about an extra $100 a year.

The government, however, says the fall in private investment will be more than offset by its taxpayer-funded boost to housing stock, which will also put downward pressure on rents longer term.

$2 billion has been committed to build more sewerage, roads and other enabling infrastructure to open up new housing lots, and is expected to bring on an additional 65,000 new homes over four years.

States will be able to access that money on the condition they agree to release more home-ready land and agree to productivity reforms to speed up housing approvals and simplify the National Construction Code.

And a temporary ban on foreign buyers will be extended by another two years to mid-2029.

Altogether, the government expects its housing measures will add 30,000 more dwellings over four years, a small extra step towards catching up to its goal of building 1.2 million new homes by the end of this decade.

In the long term, it will help fix another problem hanging over the government's head: the budget deficit.

The revenue from the government's tax package will net it an additional $77.2 billion over a decade.

But in the short term, the government expects its changes to raise $3.6 billion, which it says will mostly be paid back out in other tax relief measures such as its $250 tax offset for workers.

Albanese government breaks another tax promise

The changes to negative gearing and CGT are more broken promises not to fiddle with tax settings.

This is now the second time the government has gone to an election promising not to fiddle with a tax only to go back on its word, which it similarly did in 2022 after vowing not to amend the already-legislated stage 3 tax cuts.

On the campaign trail, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese snapped at a reporter who asked whether he could rule out changes to either tax perk, saying: "Yes. How hard is it? For the 50th time."

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to this federal budget. Have your say.

The government has calculated the popularity of curbing negative gearing and the CGT discount, which have loomed over the debate for young people locked out of the housing market, will be worth the damage to trust of breaking another promise.

Mr Chalmers conceded the government had broken its promise to voters.

"The comments we made at the election reflected, I think, the government's almost singular focus on housing supply, and we have maintained a focus in this budget on supply.

"I acknowledge this is a controversial change. I acknowledge this is a government coming to a different view than the view it held 12 months ago."

Closing trust loophole a quiet budget money-spinner

The new minimum tax rate on family trusts has received less attention in the lead-up to the federal budget but could prove a significant money maker for the government.

Discretionary trusts are designed to help protect assets and plan family succession.

But the government says some very-high-income earners use trusts to lower their tax owed by spreading the income they earn across their lower-earning family unit, meaning overall less income is taxed at the highest tax rates.

Loading

The government says the vast majority of trust income flows to the top-earning 10 per cent of families, generally to households with a net worth above $2.3 million.

From July 2028, trustees will pay a minimum 30 per cent tax rate on taxable income held in trusts, regardless of how it is spread around, and in 2029–30 alone, that is expected to raise $4.47 billion in revenue.

The government says that minimum tax closes a loophole benefiting wealthy families that the average worker is unable to use.

World.title: Find out if you're among the budget's winners or losers
World.content:
Investors are losing some of their discounts in a major overhaul of the tax system.

Under the current rules, Australians can take advantage of a 50 per cent capital gains tax discount if they hold an asset for more than 12 months.

A capital gain is the profit made from selling assets, such as investment properties, shares, crypto or even collectible items, such as artwork.

This discount was designed to encourage investment. However, critics argue the measure, combined with negative gearing, has skewed home ownership away from owner-occupiers and towards property investors.

The 50 per cent discount will be replaced by a discount based on inflation.

Investors will always pay at least 30 per cent tax on gains under a new minimum rate designed to avoid people holding on to assets until years when their income is low.

Pensioners and people on income support will be exempt from the 30 per cent minimum rate.

The new reforms will only apply to gains made after July 1, 2027, with any made before that date still qualifying for the 50 per cent discount.

To aim to encourage investment in new housing, investors who purchase new builds can choose from the 50 per cent CGT discount or the new settings when they sell their properties.

The new rules will also partially end an exemption for assets purchased before 1985.

Those Australians sitting on decades-old assets must now pay tax on gains made after July 1, 2027, using the new inflation rules.

Combined with changes to negative gearing, this measure is estimated to raise $3.6 billion over five years from 2025–26, and is expected to help 75,000 Australians buy their own home over the next decade.

World.title: Father allegedly high on 'nangs' in crash that killed daughters, as scuffle erupts outside court
World.content:
A Perth father was allegedly under the influence of nitrous oxide, or "nangs", when he crashed his car in Perth's north-eastern suburbs, killing his two young daughters and injuring their mother, a court has heard.

Jean Adrien Nathanael Luckoo, 24, appeared before the Midland Magistrates Court on Tuesday and was denied bail after facing two counts of dangerous driving causing death and one count of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm.

The girls, aged three and four, were in a Ford Territory along with Mr Luckoo and their mother heading along Muriel Street in Viveash on the afternoon of April 17 when the car left the road and smashed into a tree.

The crash happened on April 17 when police say the car left the road and hit a tree. (ABC News)

The girls suffered life-threatening injuries and were taken to Perth Children's Hospital, but died nine days later.

In court, police prosecutor Tony Freeman alleged Mr Luckoo was under the influence of nitrous oxide, known as "nangs", and that canisters were allegedly found in his vehicle.

He also alleged there was CCTV video that showed the defendant inhaling from a balloon.

Mr Luckoo also allegedly drove onto the wrong side of the road and mounted a verge, before hitting the tree.

"[The] inference therefore is the accused was intoxicated by those substances," Mr Freeman said.

Defence lawyer Mark Hager asked for his client to have a surety of $100,000 dollars, adding that he would reside with his parents.

He also told the court his client's partner was in the back of court supporting him.

"It would be on our submission, it would be wholly unfair he could not have contact with the mother of his deceased children," he said.

Scuffle outside court

As court was adjourned for a break, emotions ran high when supporters of the accused and his family clashed with waiting media as they were leaving.

A scuffle outside Midland court. (ABC News)

Vision shows Mr Luckoo's partner and the mother of his children, who was covering her face in a jacket, being escorted into the back seat of a waiting car by a male and female supporter.

The female supporter then approached a male photographer who was taking photos through the car's window.

In a physical confrontation, he grabs the woman by the neck and forces her back several steps before shoving her up a kerb.

"The f**k are you doing putting your hands on a woman, get your hands off her," her male friend yells as he steps between them.

A spokeswoman for WA Police said no complaint has been received.

Behaviour 'very concerning'

Back in court, Magistrate Paul Lyons said he was "very concerned about Mr Luckoo's recent pattern of behaviour".

The car was travelling along Muriel Street in the north-eastern Perth suburb of Viveash. (ABC News)

The magistrate said the "very nature and seriousness" of the charges gave risk to Mr Luckoo not attending future court appearances.

Magistrate Lyons also referred to a prior conviction of Mr Luckoo's for speeding and said it was still not clear whether he was on an extraordinary driver's license.

He refused Mr Luckoo's bail and remanded him in custody. He is due to face court again on June 16.

World.title: Racing appointed a new chief vet on Monday. They let him go on Tuesday
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing Racing appointed a new chief vet on Monday. They let him go on Tuesday Danny Russell May 12, 2026 — 10:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Racing Victoria has sensationally backflipped on its decision to appoint Dr Glenn Robertson-Smith as its new chief vet just one day after announcing he would be starting in the role. The embarrassing U-turn came on Tuesday after Racing Victoria was made aware that Robertson-Smith had been charged by police in 2018 for making threatening phone calls to a Melbourne Racing Club executive. Vet Dr Glenn Robertson-Smith. Racing Victoria Racing Victoria released a statement on Tuesday night, saying it would not be “proceeding with the appointment of Dr Glenn Robertson-Smith as its next chief veterinary officer”. “Based on information confirmed today we have decided we won’t be proceeding with the appointment,” RV chief executive Aaron Morrison said.





“Glenn is returning to Australia from his current role with the Hong Kong Jockey Club and will be well known to many within the industry given his extensive veterinary background in Victoria,” Stier said in a Racing Victoria press release. Safety protocols introduced by Racing Victoria in 2021 have resulted in a safer Melbourne Cup. Getty Images But by Tuesday, Stier and Morrison were working vigorously to reverse the decision. The chief veterinary officer performs a vital role, overseeing the crucial Melbourne Cup safety protocols, leading the industry’s anti-doping program and staffing 530 yearly race meetings with vets, vet nurses and swabbing officials. Racing Victoria also announced the appointment of Dr Stephanie Chapman as deputy chief veterinary officer on Monday.



Chapman will start on July 13, and will almost immediately begin screening international horses that are targeting this year’s spring racing carnival and Melbourne Cup. Dr Stephanie Chapman was announced as Racing Victoria’s deputy chief veterinary officer on Monday. Stier said on Monday the dual appointment of Robertson-Smith and Chapman “would provide great leadership to our hard-working veterinary services team who play a vital role in supporting and protecting the welfare of horses and compliance with the rules every day”. RV sent an email to staff on Tuesday night, seen by this masthead, that said, “Today we were provided with information about admissions made in a Magistrates Court matter that means that Dr Robertson-Smith’s appointment does not align with our values ... this is an unfortunate situation, and we will be conducting a review of our internal processes to ensure that they are appropriate and as rigorous as possible. “In the meantime, discussions will progress on the appointment of another chief veterinary officer.”



Forbes reached an out-of-court settlement with Racing Victoria in December after an ugly, months-long spat in which Forbes had lodged applications with the Fair Work Commission and the Federal Court. In her application to the commission for an order to stop bullying, Forbes alleged she had been pressured by Racing Victoria to become more flexible and allow international horses at “high risk of injury” to run in the Melbourne Cup. Her legal counsel, barrister Nicholas Harrington, told the Fair Work Commission his client had been “damaged” by the conduct of Racing Victoria. Racing Victoria and Morrison strongly denied the claims. Forbes headed the program that introduced strict safety protocols for the Melbourne Cup in 2021 – a fundamental shift that stopped horses suffering catastrophic injuries and dying in the race.



Robertson-Smith was seen as a highly regarded replacement. A vet for more than 40 years, he operated out of Caulfield and Cranbourne racecourses, and lectured in surgery at the University. He is a fellow of the Australian College of Veterinary Scientists in Equine Surgery, with advanced postgraduate training in Australia and the United States. World.title: Britain plunges into leadership crisis as Starmer refuses to step down
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeUK politics Britain plunges into leadership crisis as Starmer refuses to step down David Crowe Updated May 12, 2026 — 9:51pm ,first published 7:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Britain has plunged into a leadership crisis after Labour MPs went public with calls for Prime Minister Keir Starmer to quit after devastating losses in elections last Thursday, with ministers also telling him to go. Starmer raised the stakes at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday morning in London (7pm Tuesday AEST), where he told colleagues he would not resign despite the calls from more than 70 MPs for a transition to a new leader. British Prime Minister Keir Starmer has been under mounting pressure. AP His move puts the onus on his critics, including Australian-born MP Catherine West, to launch a formal leadership contest and prove they not only have a large number of MPs but can also secure a majority of party members. Starmer argued in cabinet that he took responsibility for the election result but that the party had a process for a leadership election.



“The past 48 hours have been destabilising for government, and that has a real economic cost for our country and for families,” he said. “The Labour Party has a process for challenging a leader and that has not been triggered. “The country expects us to get on with governing. That is what I am doing and what we must do as a cabinet.” While the media has reported that three cabinet ministers have advised Starmer to set out a transition to his resignation, they have not gone public. The media has named Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper as the trio who put this to the prime minister.



Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy, who is reportedly among three cabinet ministers who advised Starmer to set out a transition to his resignation, arriving for Tuesday’s meeting. AP One junior minister, Miatta Fahnbulleh, announced her resignation on Tuesday morning in London and called on Starmer to quit. “Our country faces enormous challenges and people are crying out for the scale of change that this requires,” said Fahnbulleh, whose portfolio included communities and faith. “The public does not believe that you can lead this change – and nor do I.” Junior minister Miatta Fahnbulleh, pictured right with Starmer last week, announced her resignation on Tuesday morning and called for him to go. Getty Images



Several ministers emerged from the cabinet meeting to declare their public support for Starmer and warn that the instability was rattling the financial markets and therefore increasing the interest bill on the nation’s debt. “This is not a game. This instability has consequences for people’s lives,” said Housing Secretary Steve Reed on X after the cabinet meeting. “The people who will be hurt most will be those that elected us less than two years ago. We must unite behind the Prime Minister.” Housing Secretary Steve Reed arrives for the cabinet meeting. Bloomberg Business Secretary Peter Kyle praised Starmer’s “steadfast leadership” and backed him to stay in office. The Technology Secretary, Liz Kendall, said the prime minister had her full support. The Work and Pensions Secretary, Pat McFadden, also backed Starmer when he spoke to reporters in Downing Street after the meeting.



Baroness Jenny Chapman, a Labour peer and close ally of Starmer, told Sky News after the cabinet meeting that no ministers spoke up against the prime minister. “Everybody actually acknowledged the strength of leadership that the prime minister has shown,” said Chapman, the Minister of State for International Development. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Tumult in Westminster reveals an uncomfortable truth for Labour Chapman said she believed Starmer would contest any challenge against him and would win that challenge, but she acknowledged that Labour MPs were in pain over the election results last Thursday. “I think it would be the worst thing that we could do – to embark on a kind of process that leads to instability in the leadership of this country,” she said.



“It would be bad for our economy, but bad for our politics more generally, as well, if we were to do that.” One of the ministers named most often as a leadership contender, Health Secretary Wes Streeting, made no comment to the media when he left the cabinet meeting. Health Secretary Wes Streeting departs. Getty Images The other principal contender is Andy Burnham, the left-wing mayor of Greater Manchester, but he is not in parliament and would need time to find a seat in the House of Commons before mounting a challenge. Starmer’s allies blocked him from contesting a byelection last year. Starmer prepared for the cabinet meeting by making a speech to supporters and the media on Monday morning (Monday night AEST) to warn that a leadership change would plunge the government into chaos.



“I know that people are frustrated by the state of Britain, frustrated by politics, and some people, frustrated with me,” he said. “I know I have my doubters and I know I need to prove them wrong – and I will.” He used the address, made to a relatively small group but televised live, to announce the nationalisation of British Steel and set out his plans for stronger ties with Europe. Related Article Analysis

UK ‘A horrible place’: This gloomy town shows why angry voters are lurching to the right Within hours of the address, however, more MPs went public with calls for him to set out a pathway to his resignation, and the British press reported that at least 70 wanted him to go. Labour has 403 members in the House of Commons and the party rules say that a spill can only be launched if 20 per cent of that group, which amounts to 81 in the current parliament, put their names to a formal document asking for the vote.



The formal call for a vote then triggers an election of the Labour Party membership. About 161,000 members voted in the ballot that chose Lucy Powell as deputy leader last October. By noon on Tuesday in London (9pm AEST) the British press were reporting that 81 MPs were calling for a transition to a new leader, enough to force a leadership contest. West declared on Saturday that she would stand for the leadership to trigger a vote if Starmer did not quit, but she changed tack on Monday and said she wanted a pathway to deciding a new leader by September.
